newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-High debt to keep British consumers in check.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-High debt to keep British consumers in check.

text.p: UK consumer spending is poised for further strong growth this year but with many Britons saddled with high debts and feeling less secure about their jobs, a re-run of the 1980s boom is not on the cards, economists say. Worries over more interest rate rises and a quick reversal of recent tax cuts, whichever party wins a general election due by May 22, will also play a part in dampening consumers' enthusiasm.

"Consumption is going to grow strongly this year but there are a number of factors that are going to temper consumer activity and ensure no repeat of the 1980s boom," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.
He said record levels of personal debt, lingering worries about job loss across the labour market and fears of tax and rate rises will help rein back consumption.
Roger Bootle, group chief economist at HSBC Markets, said even the perception of higher rates could be enough to choke off demand before it gets out of hand.

"The mere threat of higher interest rates could have a dampening effect. The extremely high level of consumer indebtedness means that the (risk) of higher rates probably has a far greater impact on consumer behaviour than it did, say, a decade ago."
Personal debt escalated sharply in the 1980s as credit restrictions were relaxed and helped fuel a consumer and housing boom towards the end of the decade.
But consumers have not managed to repay that debt and in many cases have allowed it to spiral even higher.

In 1983, personal sector financial liability as a percentage of disposable income was 54 percent. By 1988 it had risen to 100.5 percent and latest figures show it has grown still higher, to 107 percent at the end of the third quarter of 1996.

Sharp price rises in the housing market towards the end of the 1980s also allowed home owners to borrow against the value of their houses to finance their spending spree. Few home owners are in a position to do that now.
Bootle said the prospect of a new government after nearly two decades of Conservative rule might also restrain consumers.
"Coupled with the uncertainty caused by the first change of government in 18 years, consumers may not feel as footloose and fancy-free as some are assuming," he said.
The opposition Labour Party is leading the ruling Conservatives by around 20 points in the opinion polls.
Both major parties have gone to great lengths to convince voters that they do not intend to raise taxes but the state of public finances indicates recent tax giveaways might soon have to be reversed.
Economic growth this year will give tax revenues a boost but heavy public spending commitments mean the government will struggle to balance the budget in the medium term.
And if Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke manages to get away with leaving interest rates on hold until the election, a rate rise will be top of the agenda.

Economists also say income growth, the real fuel for high consumption, is set for only a modest pickup this year. Pay settlements data from late last year certainly suggests that wage rises are not spiralling upwards.

"Real income growth is what really anchors consumer spending and that is set to grow by around 3.0 percent this year with around one percentage point of that down to other income. It's not really the stuff booms are made of," said Philpotts.

However, this will be topped up in many households by around 17 billion pounds ($28.7 billion) worth of windfall gains from building societies and another two billion or so in maturing tax-free investments.
There is no precedent for such a huge influx of cash into the economy but analysts agree that even if only a little of the cash leaks out, it will provide quite a boost to spending.

"We are assuming these windfalls will add about 5.0 billion pounds or one percent to spending this year, particularly on consumer durables. However, the outcome is still highly uncertain," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon.
